I think you're radically underestimating the changes in worker productivity.

While technology has certainly created lots of jobs, workforce participation rates have been steadily declining very much in line with increasing productivity. Furthermore, the median income in real dollars hit its peak in the 70s. That's generally a good indicator for when the market really started to become oversaturated with qualified workers since an excess of qualified workers relative to the number of positions available tends to result in decreasing, and at best - stagnating, wages. And that was decades before outsourcing became a big thing.

And worker productivity is never going to go meaningfully down again. As we see more widespread automation it will begin to rise far more sharply than in the past. The reason this is important is because it's not only not about foreign workers, but it's also not even about domestic workers. The problem is the proportion of the population needed to produce the goods and services for everybody else continues to decline. This remains a problem whether you have a billion people, 300 million, or even just a few million. It's ultimately the thing that I think will result in a shift to a new socioeconomic system altogether.

Because boomers aren't retiring from healthcare jobs, there' a lower demand for new healthcare workers, and schools which already bottle-necked the process of getting new people into the workforce have scaled back their programs. There's going to be a lot of people retiring soon, a huge glut of incoming sicker people due to both aging boomers and the "expanding" American diet.
